grammatical_complexity.notes: Dominated by past simple narration, but past perfect and past continuous appear regularly throughout (roughly 20-25% of sentences). Participial phrases ('Unable to see anything', 'Through a series of movements') add complexity. One conditional-like structure ('If God was going to take...').

cultural_reference_load.notes: Earthquake scenario is highly familiar to Latin American learners. Cellphone earthquake alerts are common in countries like Mexico. No North American-specific customs or institutions. The political critique about politicians being rescued first resonates with LatAm readers.

sentence_structure.notes: Mixed lengths with very short punchy sentences ('Nothing.') alongside longer sentences with subordinate clauses. Narrative style uses fragments and short sentences for dramatic effect, balanced with compound-complex sentences for description.

items.context: he threw off a large piece of concrete
items.reason: Collocated with 'piece of concrete,' the meaning of big in size is clear from context. A Spanish speaker might briefly think 'largo' (long) but the physical object context disambiguates.

items.context: About the same location as his apartment
items.reason: Used to mean place/position, which is close enough to the Spanish 'locación' in this spatial context. No real confusion likely.
'Parents' is such a basic, early-learned word that most adult learners know it means father and mother, not the broader Spanish 'parientes.' Context with 'grandmother' further clarifies.

items.context: Something that said this was a test
items.reason: Spanish 'test' is borrowed from English and means exam/trial. Here it means a drill/test of the alert system. The meanings overlap sufficiently that confusion is unlikely.
